section.title: Activity

list.item: Use the graphing tool or technology outside the course. Plot some values for the length and area of the garden with perimeter 50 meters on the coordinate plane.

problem.para: Use your table, or here is a sample table of values if you need one:
problem.title: Values for a Rectangular Garden with a Perimeter of 50 Meters
problem.para: Be sure to label your axes. Select the solution button to compare your work.

image.alt: Points plotted on a grid. Area of garden, square meters. Length of garden, meters.

div.para: At first, the area grows as the length increases, but then it decreases. Also, the area increases more and more slowly as the length increases.

list.item: What do you notice about how the plotted points increase and decrease?

div.para: The point \((3, 66)\) means that if the length of the garden is 3 meters, then the area is 66 square meters. This is right because the width is 22 meters and \(3 \cdot 22=66\). The point \((22, 66)\) means that the length of the garden is 22 meters, so its width is 3 meters, and the area is again 66 square meters.

list.item: The points \((3, 66)\) and \((22, 66)\) each represent the length and area of the garden. Plot these two points on a coordinate plane, if you haven’t already done so. What do these points mean in this situation?

div.para: The point \((1, 25)\) cannot represent the length and area of the garden. If the length of the garden is 1 meter, the width would be 24 meters, so the area is 24 square meters, not 25 square meters.

list.item: Could the point \((1, 25)\) represent the length and area of the garden?

section.title: Video: The Meaning of Points on a Graph
section.para: Watch the following video to learn more about the meaning of points on a graph.

div.para: The area stays the same if the length and width are interchanged because the area is the product of the length and the width.

list.item: What happens to the area when you interchange the length and width? For example, compare the areas of a rectangle of length 11 meters and width 14 meters with a rectangle of length 14 meters and width 11 meters.

div.para: Many of the areas would come with two different pairs: for example, 100 comes from the pair \((5, 100)\) and also from the pair \((20, 100)\) because a rectangle with length 5 meters and width 20 meters is the same as a rectangle with length 20 meters and width 5 meters. Using a different length and corresponding width, the 156 comes from the pair \((12, 156)\) and also from the pair \((13, 156)\). The points on the graph would have reflectional symmetry about the line \(x=12.5\).

list.item: What patterns would you notice if you were to plot more length and area pairs on the graph?
